description: Three-mode syntax redesign — replace []-only syntax with [] juxtaposition, {} command mode, () infix mode. Clean break from old syntax, all tests rewritten.

userStories.title: Lexer — new tokens and keywords
userStories.description: As a compiler developer, I need the lexer to emit new token types for the three-mode syntax so the parser can distinguish between modes and keywords.
acceptanceCriteria: Add TOKEN_PIPE for |, TOKEN_ARROW for ->, TOKEN_BACKSLASH for \
Add TOKEN_BANG for !, TOKEN_DOTDOT for .., TOKEN_AMP for &
Add TOKEN_AND for &&, TOKEN_OR for ||, TOKEN_NOT for ~
Add TOKEN_EQUALS for =, TOKEN_COLON for :, TOKEN_DOUBLE_COLON for ::
Add TOKEN_DOLLAR_PAREN for $( in string interpolation

Add keyword tokens: TOKEN_STRUCT (replacing TOKEN_DEFSTRUCT), TOKEN_PROC, TOKEN_IF, TOKEN_ELIF, TOKEN_ELSE, TOKEN_WHILE, TOKEN_FOR, TOKEN_DEF, TOKEN_MUT, TOKEN_SET, TOKEN_MATCH, TOKEN_RETURN, TOKEN_BREAK, TOKEN_CONTINUE, TOKEN_TRY
Remove TOKEN_DEFSTRUCT
Existing token types (TOKEN_WORD, TOKEN_INT, TOKEN_FLOAT, TOKEN_STRING, TOKEN_VAR, TOKEN_LBRACKET, TOKEN_RBRACKET, etc.) still work unchanged
All new tokens have correct source position tracking (line, column, byte offset)
Rewrite test_lexer.c to test all new token types
All existing tests still pass (no regressions)
userStories.notes: This is additive — old token types still work. The parser hasn't changed yet so old syntax still parses. Keywords are recognized by the lexer in the word-scanning path (similar to how TOKEN_USE and TOKEN_DEFSTRUCT are handled today at lexer.c lines 960-970). New operator tokens (|, ->, &&, ||, ~, =, :, ::) need to be recognized in the operator-scanning path.

userStories.title: Parser — infix mode for ()
userStories.description: As a compiler developer, I need the parser to handle () as infix mode where operators are parsed left-to-right with no precedence.
acceptanceCriteria: ($x + 3) parses as AST_COMMAND with head +, args $x and 3
($x + 3 * 2) parses as AST_COMMAND [* [+ $x 3] 2] — no precedence, left-to-right
(1 + (2 * 3)) parses as [+ 1 [* 2 3]] — explicit grouping with nested parens
Unary prefix operators bind tighter: (- $x + $y) parses as [+ [neg $x] $y]
All arithmetic operators work in infix: +, -, *, /, %
All comparison operators work in infix: ==, <, >, <=, >=
Logical operators: ($a && $b) parses as [and $a $b], ($a || $b) as [or $a $b], (~ $a) as [not $a]
Nested [] calls work inside (): ($x + [vec-len $v]) parses correctly
Variable references work: ($x + $y) parses correctly
Add parser tests for all infix patterns
All existing tests still pass (no regressions)
userStories.notes: This is additive — () was previously unused in the parser. Create a new parser__parse_infix() function. The key algorithm: parse first operand, then loop: if next token is an operator, parse next operand, wrap in AST_COMMAND with operator as head. For unary prefix (- and ~), check if the first token is an operator and handle it before entering the binary loop. and/or/not don't exist as builtins yet — parse them as command names and defer compilation to a later story.

userStories.title: Proc syntax update

acceptanceCriteria: proc foo {x, y} {+ $x $y} — braces for both params and body
proc i64 add {i64 a, i64 b} {+ $a $b} — return type before name, typed params
proc greet {} {print "hello"} — zero-arg procs with empty param braces
proc add {a, b} {+ $a $b} — untyped params (gradual typing preserved)
Params are comma-separated within {}
Type-before-name in params: {i64 a, str b} not {a :i64, b :str}
Closures and upvalue capture still work with new syntax
Tail-call optimization still applies with new syntax
Old proc syntax [proc [x y] [+ $x $y]] still works (backward compat during transition)
New-syntax proc tests added and passing
All existing tests still pass (no regressions)
userStories.notes: The parser needs to detect when proc is followed by a word (name) then { (params). Parse the param list as comma-separated items, where each item is either 'type name' (two words) or 'name' (one word). The body is the next {} block parsed in command mode (bare commands). The compiler receives the same AST_COMMAND structure it handles today — just constructed differently by the parser. Keep the old [proc [params] [body]] path working during transition.

userStories.title: Control flow — if/elif/else and while
userStories.description: As a compiler developer, I need if to support block bodies with elif chains and while to use block bodies, while keeping old syntax working temporarily.
acceptanceCriteria: if $cond { body } — condition then block
if $cond { body } else { body } — else clause
if $cond { body } elif $cond2 { body } else { body } — elif chains
if with infix condition: if ($n > 0) { "positive" } else { "non-positive" }
if is an expression — returns value of the taken branch
while $cond { body } — while loop with block body
while ($i < 10) { body } — while with infix condition
Old [if cond then else] syntax still works (backward compat during transition)
New-syntax control flow tests added and passing
All existing tests still pass (no regressions)
userStories.notes: The parser detects if keyword, parses condition (which can be a $var, a () infix expression, or a [] command), then parses { body } block. If next token is elif, repeat. If next token is else, parse final { body }. The elif chain desugars to nested if/else in the AST. The compiler already handles if with 2 or 3 args — the parser just needs to produce the right AST shape.

userStories.title: for command replacing each
userStories.description: As a compiler developer, I need for to replace each as the iteration command, with implicit $it binding and explicit name binding forms.
acceptanceCriteria: for $items { print $it } — iteration with implicit $it binding
for $items item { print $item } — iteration with explicit binding variable
for $items [\  print $it] — iteration with lambda callback (HOF form, like current each)
Compiler distinguishes forms by argument shape: value+block = implicit $it, value+word+block = explicit binding, value+closure = HOF callback
for works on vectors (same runtime behavior as current each)
each still works as alias for for during transition
New-syntax for tests added and passing
All existing tests still pass (no regressions)
userStories.notes: The HOF callback form (for $items callback) maps directly to current each behavior — same opcode (OP_EACH). The block forms (implicit $it and explicit binding) are new — the compiler needs to wrap the block body in an implicit closure with the binding variable, then emit OP_EACH. The parser detects for keyword and determines which form based on what follows the collection argument.

userStories.title: Binding operators (=, :, ::)
userStories.description: As a compiler developer, I need =, :, :: to work as sugar for def, mut, set in command mode.
acceptanceCriteria: x = 5 desugars to [def x 5]

x : 0 desugars to [mut x 0]

Command forms def/mut/set still work alongside operators

Tests for all binding operator forms passing

userStories.notes: The desugaring happens in the parser or early compiler: when parsing a command in {} mode, after collecting tokens, scan for =, :, or :: operators. If found, rewrite the command as a def/mut/set AST_COMMAND. For typed bindings like 'i64 x = 5', the type word and name word appear before the operator. The parser needs to handle this without ambiguity — = and : should only be treated as binding operators when they appear in the right position (after a name or type+name).

userStories.title: Arrow field access (->)

acceptanceCriteria: $point->x parses as field access and compiles to OP_STRUCT_GET
Works in all three modes: $point->x in {}, ($point->x + 1) in (), [foo $point->x] in []

userStories.notes: The -> can be handled in the parser as a postfix operator on expressions. After parsing a primary expression ($var, [cmd], etc.), check if the next token is TOKEN_ARROW. If so, consume the arrow and the following word (field name), and wrap in an AST_COMMAND equivalent to [. expr field]. Chain by looping. This is similar to how many languages handle member access as a postfix operator.

userStories.title: Pipe threading (|)
userStories.description: As a compiler developer, I need | in command mode to thread the left command's result as the first argument to the right command.
acceptanceCriteria: foo $a | bar $b desugars to [bar [foo $a] $b] (first-arg threading)
Multi-stage pipes: a | b | c desugars to [c [b [a]]]
Pipes with arguments: + 1 2 | * 3 desugars to [* [+ 1 2] 3]
Pipes compose with existing builtins: vec 1 2 3 | vec-len desugars to [vec-len [vec 1 2 3]]
Pipe short-circuits on error values (existing error propagation via OP_CHECK_ERROR handles this)
Tests for pipe threading passing
All existing tests still pass (no regressions)
userStories.notes: Pipes are parsed in command mode when TOKEN_PIPE appears between commands. The parser collects left-side command, sees |, collects right-side command, then rewrites: right command's args list gets left command's result inserted as first arg. This is an AST rewrite — the compiler never sees pipes, just nested AST_COMMAND nodes. Implement in the parser's command-mode parsing function.

acceptanceCriteria: [\ + $it 2] parses as equivalent to [proc {it} {+ $it $2}] — lambda with implicit $it

userStories.notes: In the parser, when parsing inside [] and the first token is TOKEN_BACKSLASH, treat the remaining items as the body of a proc with a single param named 'it'. Construct an AST equivalent to [proc [it] [body...]]. The compiler already handles proc/closure compilation — the parser just needs to produce the right AST. Disambiguation from line continuation: \ followed by newline = continuation; \ followed by non-newline inside [] = lambda.

userStories.notes: For $(expr): the lexer already handles $[ for TOKEN_DOLLAR_BRACKET. Add similar handling for $( — emit TOKEN_DOLLAR_PAREN. The parser, when building an interpolated string and encountering TOKEN_DOLLAR_PAREN, calls parser__parse_infix() to parse the infix expression, then expects TOKEN_RPAREN. For line continuation: in the lexer, when \ is followed by newline, skip both and continue scanning. This only applies when not inside [] (where \ is lambda shorthand).
